title: Excerpt of the area around RSCG 55
caption: The galaxy pair NGC 4411a and NGC 4411b with RSCG 55, imaged by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory
celestial: NGC 4411, RSCG 55, Vera C. Rubin Observatory · constellation Virgo

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Two spiral galaxies swirl through this small section of one of the First Look images captured by the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Although NGC 4411b, on the left, and NGC 4411a, on the right, appear side by side, they show no signs of interacting, such as distorted arms.

Higher up in the frame sits RSCG 55, a group of galaxies that are interacting, linked by trails of material. Those trails are made of stars, gas and dust pulled from one galaxy to another during an earlier close encounter.

Galaxies that appear next to each other on the sky are not necessarily close in space; one may lie far behind the other along the same line of sight. Distorted arms, bridges and tails are the telltale signs astronomers look for when judging whether galaxies are truly interacting. This view was taken with the LSST Camera on Rubin's Simonyi Survey Telescope, looking toward the constellation Virgo.
